title: 1948–1957: The First Postwar Decade
tagline: Affluent society · Golden age of manufacturing · Three recessions · Wartime mobilization and postwar transition

sections.heading: Era Tone
body: In this postwar decade, US industrial production grew at an average monthly year-over-year rate of 5.0%, but with sharp swings: the low was −9.4% and the high 27.5%, while the NBER identified three recessions. This was a decade of expansion through turmoil — bracketed on one end by the Marshall Plan and the final stretch of wartime controls, and on the other by the rise of the postwar affluent society. Over the decade, nominal GDP rose 89.9%, pre-tax corporate profits rose 56.9%, and after-tax profits 41.4%. The macro picture ran far ahead of the micro one, because wartime tax rates and price controls kept squeezing corporate earnings.

items.body: CPI was still 8.1% in 1948 and the Fed raised reserve requirements three times in a year to fight inflation. A mild recession (the first postwar downturn) hit in 1949. The Korean War broke out in 1950: companies borrowed heavily to ramp production and stockpile inventory, and CPI swung from negative to 5.9% in six months.

Government consumption's contribution to GDP jumped from zero in 1950 to 6.2 percentage points in 1951 — the second-highest postwar reading. The 1951 Treasury–Fed Accord was signed, and the Federal Reserve began operating as a genuinely independent central bank — a pivotal turning point in 20th-century monetary-policy history.

The 1953 armistice and the resulting defense-spending cuts triggered a recession (NBER: Jul 1953 – May 1954). GDP fell 0.6% in 1954. In 1955, consumer spending and capex jointly pulled GDP back to +7.1% — a textbook move from recovery to boom.

GDP growth slipped from 7.1% in 1955 to 2.1% in 1956. From August 1957 the economy entered the first postwar globally synchronized recession (NBER: Aug 1957 – Apr 1958): industrial output fell across the major capitalist economies, with steel and auto production down 14.2% and 9.5% respectively.

sections.heading: Economic Structure: A Golden Age for Manufacturing
body: This was the decade in which US manufacturing's position as the largest sector of the economy was most firmly entrenched. By the end of 1957, manufacturing value added reached 27% of GDP, two points higher than 1947's 25%, and 13 points ahead of the second-largest sector, wholesale and retail trade. Reconstruction in Western Europe gave US manufacturers a vast external market.

But the structure was quietly shifting. The primary sector (agriculture, forestry, fishing) fell from 8% of GDP in 1947 to 4% in 1957; finance and real estate rose from 10% to 13%; business services and information industries also grew in importance. On profits, overseas income grew at an annualized 21.4% — far above any domestic industry, marking the start of the era of large US multinational profits.

Inside manufacturing, durables overtook nondurables. From 1948 to 1957, other transportation equipment (aerospace, aviation, ships) led with a 17.8% annualized nominal growth rate; autos and parts grew 9.4%, chemicals 10.2%, and computers/electronics 9.4%. Textiles (−0.3%), apparel and leather goods (+2.8%), and wood products (+2.9%) were the laggards.

sections.heading: Wartime Controls and a High-Tax Regime
body: The Defense Production Act of 1950 enshrined the priority of defense production. The Revenue Acts of 1950 and 1951 sharply raised corporate taxes in two consecutive years. The US effective corporate tax rate jumped from 33% in 1949 to 40% in 1950, then to a historical peak of 49% in 1951. It eased to 41% by 1957, but corporate after-tax profits remained suppressed throughout the decade — the core reason for the divergence between strong macro performance and weaker corporate results.

items.body: Approximately $13 billion in aid was channeled to Europe (about 5% of 1948 US GDP), while opening postwar European markets to US manufacturers.
items.title: Marshall Plan Launched

items.body: The first postwar 'limited war' — neither a victory nor a defeat — left lasting marks on monetary policy, taxation, industry, and inflation.
items.title: –1953: Korean War

items.body: The Federal Reserve was no longer required to peg Treasury yields and formally became an independent monetary authority.
items.title: Treasury–Fed Accord

items.body: Authorized the Interstate Highway System, originally planned at $25 billion over twelve years; the final program cost $114 billion and took thirty-five years (completed in 1991). It directly fueled long bull markets in suburbanization, autos, and real estate.
items.title: Federal-Aid Highway Act

items.body: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, marking America's first setback in the satellite race; the same year, the Little Rock crisis in Arkansas ignited the civil rights movement. Wall Street also began circulating the maxim 'Don't sell on strike news.'
items.title: Sputnik and Little Rock
